title: Arrival-shape adaptive scheduling notes
body:
Context:
This is a working note for an alternative approach to sizing concurrency and continuous-batching parameters by explicitly modeling arrival-shape heterogeneity (microbursts vs steady), and mapping those shapes to p95 latency targets and incremental cost. Goal is a compact spreadsheet that product and infra PMs can use to trade latency SLOs against incremental GPU hours and amortized token cost.

Summary of approach:
- Instead of a single Poisson/steady arrival model, we parameterize incoming traffic by a 3-part shape: baseline rate (r_base), burst amplitude (r_peak_factor), and burst duration distribution (t_burst_mean, t_burst_sd).
- For each (r_base, r_peak_factor, t_burst_mean) tuple we simulate an event-based queue with the existing continuous-batching window behavior and N-server concurrency. We compute throughput, p50/p95/p99 latency, and GPU active time.
- The spreadsheet is organized around a scenario grid: rows are concurrency (N) choices and columns are batch-window choices (window_ms) and batch cap (max_batch). Each cell contains derived metrics: expected p95, avg tokens/sec, GPU utilization, and incremental cost delta vs a baseline.

Key assumptions (explicit):
- Model token generation is 1-step policy: model_ms_per_token is profiled (e.g., 12 ms/token for trimmed 13B on A100) and is a function of effective_batch_size for some kernels. We allow a ramping function: model_ms_per_token(batch) = base_ms / (1 + alpha * log(1 + batch)).
- Continuous-batching: window_ms waits up to window_ms or until early-exit max_batch reached. Arrival within window adds to same batch.
- Concurrency N is number of simultaneous in-flight model prompt+generate invocations; system schedules batches to idle servers immediately.
- Queue discipline is FIFO with tokenized service time (we convert request length to expected service time by tokens * model_ms_per_token(batch)).
- KV cache hits: for multi-turn flows we assume a fractional cache hit rate h that reduces effective tokens to generate by (1 - h).

Spreadsheet column/field definitions (what to include in the sheet):
- scenario_id (string): short id like base_lowburst_t10
- r_base_rps (float): baseline requests/sec
- burst_factor (float): multiplier for peak relative to r_base
- t_burst_mean_ms (float) and t_burst_sd_ms (float)
- conv_N (int): concurrency tested
- window_ms (int): continuous batching window in ms
- max_batch (int)
- avg_effective_batch (float): empirical from sim or analytic approx
- model_ms_per_token (float): ms per token at avg batch (formula cell)
- avg_tokens_per_request (float)
- service_time_ms (float): avg_tokens_per_request * model_ms_per_token
- arrival_variance_factor (float): captures burstiness, used in queueing approx (Cv^2)
- p95_latency_ms_sim (float): p95 from discrete-event sim
- p95_latency_ms_approx (float): M/G/N or diffusion approx value (helpful to sanity check)
- gpu_util_pct (float)
- gpu_hours_per_100k_requests (float)
- incremental_cost_usd_per_100k (float): using current price table (e.g., $X/hr)
- notes (string)

Core formulas (spreadsheet-friendly):
- model_ms_per_token(batch) = base_ms / (1 + alpha * LN(1 + batch))  -- cell formula example using LN
- effective_batch = MIN(max_batch, 1 + floor(window_ms * r_effective)) where r_effective accounts for burst shape; for approximation use expected arrivals in window = r_avg * (window_ms/1000)
- service_rate_mu = 1000 / service_time_ms (requests/sec per server)
- utilization_rho = r_arrival / (N * mu)
- p95 latency (M/G/N diffusion approx) ≈ Wq + service_time where Wq ≈ (rho^(sqrt(2*(N+1))) * CV^2) * (service_time/(1-rho)) * calibration_factor -- note: this is a heuristic cell that we calibrate against sim outputs

Example scenarios (sample numbers in sheet to illustrate):
- Scenario A (steady low): r_base=5 rps, burst_factor=1.2 t_burst=5s. Expect avg_batch ~1-2 at window_ms=8ms, N=4, p95~120ms, gpu_util~12%
- Scenario B (microbursts): r_base=3 rps, burst_factor=8x, t_burst_mean=300ms. With window_ms=20ms and max_batch=32, N=6, sim p95 spiking to 420ms unless we increase N or reduce window_ms
- Scenario C (sustained surge): r_base=50 rps, burst_factor=1.5, t_burst_mean=60s. Here batching helps amortize cost; p95 depends more on baseline throughput and less on window_ms once batches are large.

Observations from early sims (quick takeaways):
- Microbursts (sub-second, high amplitude) are the worst for p95 under continuous batching because window_ms aggregates many arrivals into a few batches that then queue behind long service times; reducing window_ms reduces p95 but increases per-token CPU/GPU overhead and can lower batch efficiency.
- Increasing N gives better tail behavior up to a point, but GPU utilization falls off; optimal N balances p95 vs cost, and depends strongly on burst duration distribution.
- For multi-tenant workloads with correlated microbursts across tenants, smart routing (spill-to-cheaper-variant or region) reduces p95 spikes more cost-effectively than simply overprovisioning N.

Tradeoff visualization recommended in the sheet:
- For each scenario, produce a small heatmap: X-axis = window_ms (4ms, 8ms, 20ms, 50ms), Y-axis = N (1..12); cell color = p95 latency; overlay glyph for cost delta. This gives immediate knob tradeoffs for SRE/PM.

Calibration plan and experiments to run:
1) Build a parameterized discrete-event sim (we have a lightweight Python sim in repo referenced in linked_artifacts). Instrument to export avg_batch distribution, queue length time series, and per-request latency percentiles.
2) Sweep r_base in {1,5,20,50}, burst_factor in {2,4,8,16}, t_burst in {50ms, 300ms, 2s, 30s}. Sweep window_ms in {4,8,20,50} and N in 1..12 and max_batch in {8,16,32,64}.
3) Fit calibration_factor for the M/G/N heuristic per model family and instance type. Store coefficients in a small table used by the spreadsheet for quick approximations.
4) Validate against a small production trace (obfuscated) for one customer who has microbursty traffic (ask Privacy/Compliance for safe sample).

Open questions / decisions:
- Should spreadsheet expose CV^2 or infer it from burst params? My recommendation: show CV^2 as hidden cell and present a simple slider for burstiness for non-technical users.
- How aggressively should we suggest autoscaling policies vs static N? We should present: conservative SLO (overprovision N by +25%), cost-optimized (N that minimizes $/p95 tradeoff), and hybrid (autoscale with fast cooldown + spillover model).
- Where to place recommended default knobs by offering tier? e.g., Starter: window_ms=8ms, max_batch=16, N=4; Performance: window_ms=4ms, max_batch=32, N=8. Need to back with numbers.

Next steps (short):
- [ ] Wire up the sim sweep and export CSVs to the sheet (Marco)
- [ ] Add calibration table and implement heuristic cells (Evan)
- [ ] Run validation on sample prod trace and record divergence (Anika)
- [ ] Draft short one-pager for console UI: give SLO slider that maps to recommended window_ms/N combos and cost impact (product)

Notes to self: keep the sheet intentionally opinionated — small set of well-defined knobs and scenario presets. Users will misuse freeform grids; we ship presets and an "advanced" tab for deep tuning.

Raw experiment log snippet (for traceability):
- sim run 2025-03-01T11:42Z, model=trimmed-13B, base_ms=11.6, alpha=0.28, r_base=3, burst_factor=8, t_burst_mean=300ms, window_ms=20, max_batch=32, N=6 -> p95=428ms, gpu_util=37%, gpu_hours/100k=4.6, notes=high tail due to multi-batch buildup
- sim run 2025-03-01T12:08Z, same params but window_ms=8 -> p95=210ms, gpu_hours/100k=5.1 (cost up ~11%), notes=tail improved but cost increased


This doc is intentionally informal; keep iterating. If folks want, I can add a quick sample sheet export with pivot-ready columns and a simple heatmap chart config.
